Aquifers below the Tongue River that probably discharge northward to the Yellowstone River are the Lebo shale aquifer and the Tullock-Hell Creek aquifer. The Lebo Shale member of Fort Union Formation includes few water-bearing sandstone beds and the contained water is normally too highly mineralized to be usable for either stock or domestic supplies (U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs, 1975, p. 131). The transmissivity of the Hell Creek Formation in the southern Powder River area is reported to be 1,500 to 4,700 gpd/ft. A storage coefficient of 4 x 10<sup>-4</sup> was estimated (U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs, 1974, p. 88). According to the literature, nearby deeper aquifers belonging to the regional flow system from the Bighorn Mountains to the Powder River Basin are: the Parkman Sandstone (U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs 1974, p. 88); the Cloverly Formation -- particularly its basal conglomeratic sandstone unit; the Amsden Formation, the Madison Limestone; and the Red River Formation (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 1, pp 21, 22).
Throughout Bighorn County, the Cloverly Formation is reported to yield moderate to large quantities of water to wells tapping its basal sandstone. The potentiometric head of this unit is reported to be above ground surface southeast and southwest of the project area (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 1, p. 21).
The Amsden and Madison aquifers result from solution of the carbonate rock. A well in the Amsden Formation in Bighorn County indicated that the Amsden had a relatively high yield potential (U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, 1972, p. 54).
